title: What is @TransactionalEventListener? Explain the BEFORE_COMMIT, AFTER_COMMIT, and AFTER_ROLLBACK phases, how it differs from @EventListener, and what fallbackExecution does.
keyPoints: @TransactionalEventListener ties an event handler to a specific phase of the transaction lifecycle instead of running immediately
AFTER_COMMIT runs only after a successful commit and is the safest phase for external side effects like SMS or Kafka
BEFORE_COMMIT runs while the transaction is still open and throwing there triggers a rollback
AFTER_ROLLBACK runs only on rollback for failure logging and compensation
A plain @EventListener runs synchronously when publishEvent is called, regardless of whether the TX later commits or rolls back
fallbackExecution=true makes the handler run immediately when no active transaction exists, instead of being silently dropped

s1_definition.oneliner: @TransactionalEventListener ties an event handler to the transaction outcome so side effects like SMS or email fire only when the transaction truly commits, preventing false confirmations.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **@TransactionalEventListener** -- a Spring annotation that defers an event handler to a specific phase of the surrounding transaction's lifecycle rather than executing it immediately.
- **TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT** -- the handler runs only after the transaction commits successfully, making it the correct place for external side effects.
- **TransactionPhase.BEFORE_COMMIT** -- the handler runs just before commit while the transaction is still open, so throwing here triggers a rollback.
- **TransactionPhase.AFTER_ROLLBACK** -- the handler runs only if the transaction rolled back, used for failure logging and compensation.
- **fallbackExecution** -- when set to `true`, the handler runs immediately if no active transaction exists, instead of being silently dropped.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh transfers money to Priya at the National Bank of India, the bank publishes an internal note that says "transfer happened." With a plain @EventListener, the SMS team sends Rajesh a success text the moment the note is written, even if the transfer later fails and gets reversed. With @TransactionalEventListener set to AFTER_COMMIT, the SMS team waits until the ledger is actually stamped and final before sending the text, so the customer never gets a false confirmation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The @TransactionalEventListener annotation lets an event handler run at a specific phase of the surrounding transaction instead of immediately when the event is published. The AFTER_COMMIT phase is the most important: it fires only after a successful commit, so external side effects like SMS and Kafka messages never lie to the customer. BEFORE_COMMIT fires while the transaction is still open, so work done there is atomic with the main operation. AFTER_ROLLBACK fires only on failure for logging and compensation.

The difference from a plain @EventListener is the whole point. A plain listener runs synchronously the instant publishEvent is called, before the transaction commits. In the National Bank of India transfer system, that meant Rajesh sometimes received a success SMS for a transfer that actually rolled back. Moving the SMS handler to AFTER_COMMIT eliminated false confirmations entirely, because the handler fires only when the money movement is truly durable.

The critical gotcha is fallbackExecution. By default, if the event is published when there is no active transaction, the handler is silently dropped. Setting fallbackExecution to true makes it run immediately, which is useful for notification listeners that should work regardless of transactional context. For AFTER_COMMIT handlers, always consider pairing with @Async to avoid blocking the request thread, and use REQUIRES_NEW if the handler needs to write to the database.

Remember one sentence: use AFTER_COMMIT for anything that talks to the outside world so you never lie to the customer.
